extracted.intended_audience: military officers, War Department administrators, and government legal advisers
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and legal standards governing U.S. Army officers' acceptance of civil employment, assignments, resignations, dismissals, and related status questions under statutes (e.g., §§1222, 1224, 1228, 1229 R.S.) and executive/war powers. Covers what counts as a civil office, temporary employment, military occupation exceptions, and procedural effect of resignations and dismissals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of assignment does not vacate Regular officer's commission
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptance of an assignment as provided (e.g., assignment to volunteer Army staff service) does not vacate a Regular officer's commission; nomination and confirmation are not required when Regular officers are 'assigned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that acceptance of an assignment would not vacate a Regular officer's commission and that nomination/confirmation is not required for Regular officers so assigned. (G. 449, May 19, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: President cannot appoint Regular officer to volunteer office absent statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of statutory authority the President cannot appoint a Regular officer to office in any volunteer force that may be called out from the District of Columbia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a limitation on executive appointment power where Congress has not provided authority. (C. 4119, May 12, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Private teaching positions do not necessarily vacate commission
rubrics_metrics.description: An Army surgeon may accept a position as teacher in a private medical college without vacating his commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that a surgeon can accept such private employment. (C. 18017, Oct. 23, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments to civil public health duties in occupied territories may be military
rubrics_metrics.description: A surgeon may be assigned for duty in the office of the head of the Department of Health of Puerto Rico; health conditions of Army and people are interdependent, creating sufficient military motive to support the detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments of this kind in occupied territory are treated as military duty. (C. 18017, Mar. 16 and June 8, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorary public service not tantamount to holding an office
rubrics_metrics.description: An Army surgeon could accept appointment as an honorary member of a Puerto Rico commission without vacating his commission, since such membership lacks tenure, duration, fees, emoluments, rights, powers or duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorary memberships not involving office-like attributes do not trigger vacatur under section 1222. (C. 18017, July 28, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary municipal employment by presidential detail is not civil office
rubrics_metrics.description: An engineer officer, employed (with Secretary of War approval) to devise and provide a sewerage system for a city/county, when designated as temporary employment, is not an appointment to civil office under section 1222 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such work was distinguished from a civil office and treated as temporary employment (cases cited: P. 54, 64, June 1892; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: State municipal employment as 'employment' not 'office' if incidental and temporary
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment by a state/local board (e.g., board of water commissioners) of an Army engineer as an engineer or consulting engineer is employment merely, of a temporary and incidental character, and not a civil office within section 1222, when authorized by the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is whether the position requires separation from corps or interferes with military duties (R. 37,040; R. 43,307; 52,271; C. 19979).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers may invest private funds and serve as corporate directors if duties unimpaired
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer may legally invest private funds in corporate securities and may serve as a director in a business corporation, provided performance of military duties is not impaired or prevented by such service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible even if the corporation may later stand as a vendor to a government department. (C. 22765, Feb. 17, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical Corps officers may contract to render medical services locally
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Medical Corps may render medical services to prisoners in a nearby jail as a purely contractual arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such service is contractual and does not amount to holding a civil office. (C. 27213, Aug. 29, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting employment for municipal boards may be accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: An engineer officer may accept employment as consulting engineer for municipal bodies (e.g., Board of Estimate and Apportionment of New York City).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acceptance treated as employment; see C. 25912, Dec. 7, 1909.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1222 prohibition applies to civil offices within U.S. territorial/legislative jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on Army officers holding civil office embodied in section 1222 R.S. applies to civil office within the territorial and legislative jurisdiction of the United States and Congress, not to performance of civil duties by officers in occupied territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because military occupation is incident to command and within Presidential authority, assignments in occupied foreign territory are military duty and not civil office. (C. 5771, Feb. 1899; 20396, Apr. 17, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers assigned to civil functions in occupied territories are not entitled to additional compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers assigned to duties such as collectors of customs in Cuba and Puerto Rico during military occupation were assigned to military duty and may not receive additional compensation for execution of such duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments were considered part of military service; no extra pay allowed. (C. 5771, Feb. 2, 1899.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached or detailed officers retain pay and emoluments during temporary reassignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer detached from his office by lawful military order to perform temporary duties elsewhere remains entitled to his salary and emoluments by law and will not undergo reduction of pay because of temporary detachment; duties of his office are performed by a successor or detailed officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An order assigning an officer to temporary performance of another military office is a lawful military order which must be obeyed; the detailed officer does not become entitled to higher pay unless expressly authorized by law. (C. 16906, Sept. 26, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: President/Secretary may assign officers to duty in military occupation/governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The President or the Secretary of War has power to assign officers to any duty properly within the scope of their office, including duties connected with military occupation and administration of government in occupied territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments for military government administration (e.g., Manila) are lawful; details to civil governor for 'important military duties' treated as detached military service. (C. 16906; C. 20251, Aug. 21, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detail to purely civil duties requires congressional authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional authority to command the Army does not extend to detaching officers for the performance of purely civil duties; details of that character must be specially authorized by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where details to purely civil duty are claimed, special statutory provision is necessary; where statute provides cooperation (e.g., in Philippine government), certain details are treated as military in nature. (C. 20251, Aug. 21, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive cannot create treaty office positions by unilateral detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a treaty creates a commission (e.g., International Boundary Commission), the Executive cannot create additional offices under that commission (e.g., 'associate member'); instead an officer may be assigned advisory military duty not inconsistent with military status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested assignment as military advisory duty rather than appointment to a treaty-created 'office'. (C. 2236, Apr. 26, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailing engineers to state/civil works is constrained by §1224 if it separates them from corps
rubrics_metrics.description: While an engineer detailed by the President to assist state/municipal authorities is not exercising a civil office, section 1224 raises the question whether such work will require separation from the corps or otherwise interfere with performance of military duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the employment would separate him from his regiment/corps for any considerable period it would be unauthorized absent statutory sanction. (R. 37,540; R. 52,271; P. 49, Sept. 1891.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer/tender of resignation is revocable until acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere offer to resign or tender of resignation is revocable at any time before acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After acceptance and before effect given by notice, the offer cannot be withdrawn or materially modified by the officer alone; consent of appointing power is necessary. (C. 25005, Jan. 4, 1910; R. 39,375, Jan. 5, 1878.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of resignation fixes vacation date as date of notification
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer vacates an office by resignation; the date of vacation is the date of notification to the officer of the acceptance of his resignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification may be actual or constructive. If acceptance forwarded in the regular way to the officer's station it is presumed delivered if he was present; if absent without authority, receipt at proper station is constructive delivery. (Multiple cases cited: P.36, Nov.1889; C.15493, Nov.13,1903, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of successor operates as acceptance of resignation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the President appoints a successor without formally accepting a resignation by letter, the appointment of the successor is in effect the acceptance of the resignation, and the officer vacates upon actual or constructive notice of such appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation of acceptance after notice does not restore officer to office
rubrics_metrics.description: After an officer has been notified of acceptance of his resignation, a revocation of the acceptance will not operate to return him to office; return requires a new appointment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resignation accepted to take effect in futuro is beyond recall once officer notified
rubrics_metrics.description: Where resignation was accepted to take effect at a future date and the officer, after receiving notice of acceptance but before the fixed date, attempted to withdraw, such withdrawal should not be considered; service of notice fixed his status beyond recall as vacating on the specified date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance wording can include reasons that become part of acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's acceptance of resignation may accompany remarks or reasons considered necessary for military discipline; such reasons assigned become an essential part of the acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to reviewing authority of a court-martial; C. 16183, May 7, 1904.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unqualified acceptance = honorable discharge; 'for the good of the service' = without honor
rubrics_metrics.description: An unqualified acceptance of a resignation is an honorable discharge. Where the acceptance is 'for the good of the service' the discharge is 'without honor.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal sentence of dismissal takes effect upon official communication to officer
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal sentence of dismissal, when finally confirmed by competent authorities, takes effect upon the officer on the day the confirmation is officially communicated to him, either by promulgation at his station or other official notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the date of actual confirmation is not necessarily the date dismissal goes into effect; delays can occur (e.g., if officer is a prisoner). (R.36, Dec.1874; P.49, Sept.1891; C.16823, Sept.13,1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence of dismissal cannot be confirmed to take effect retroactively
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence of dismissal cannot legally be confirmed so as to take effect as of a date prior to that of the formal confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: If dismissal sentence illegal there has been no legal dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence of dismissal is not legal (e.g., court illegally constituted, without jurisdiction, insufficient members, members unsworn) there has been no dismissal in law; this can be declared at any time in orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An officer cannot be dismissed pursuant to a legal sentence until it is approved or confirmed by competent authority. (Multiple citations: R.20; 26; 28; 29; 30; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal by executive order is distinct from dismissal by sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal by executive order (removal) is distinct from dismissal by sentence (punishment); statutory law has limited the President's power to dismiss in time of peace, reserving certain dismissals to wartime or other statutory authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically used in Civil War; statutory constraints now apply. (C.13323; C.13654; discussion of acts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary dismissal via boards under war statutes may be lawful without sworn members or evidence record
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards appointed under certain wartime statutes to provide for temporary increases in military establishment are summary proceedings not required by statute or regulation to be sworn or to record evidence; their reports, when approved by the President, can render discharges legal even without those formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from boards under other acts where members were sworn. (discussion re: act of April 22, 1898; C.4842, Aug. 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary dismissal does not take effect until order delivered or officer officially notified
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary dismissal of an officer does not properly take effect until the order of dismissal or an official copy is delivered to him, or he is otherwise officially notified of the dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: President may fix a future operative date for dismissal; acts remain legal until notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The President, when dismissing an officer by order, may fix a future date when the discharge becomes operative; until the officer receives notice acts of the officer are legal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a future date is fixed, department orders cannot make discharge effective as of an earlier date. (C.16823, Sept.13,1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary dismissal by Secretary of War is legally the act of the President
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary dismissal 'by order of the Secretary of War' is in law the act of the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department/Army commanders lack authority to summarily dismiss officers except in historic wartime practice ratified by appointment of successor
rubrics_metrics.description: A department or Army commander has no authority to summarily dismiss or discharge an officer; but where such authority was actually exercised historically and the President made the dismissal his own by appointing a successor, the dismissal was validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R.11; 16; 41; 42; P.47; examples given of Civil War practice where subsequent action by appointing authority validated the dismissal. (R.41 Jan.1878; R.44 July 1880; C.3728.)

rubrics_metrics.name: De facto officer doctrine protects acts of a subsequently validated incumbent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a dismissed officer's sentence is later found illegal and the previously mustered-in successor acted as officer, the successor is a de facto officer and his acts affecting third parties are legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal by sentence does not permanently bar eligibility for appointment or civil office
rubrics_metrics.description: Dismissal by sentence of a general court-martial does not render an officer ineligible for future appointment to military office, enlistment as a soldier, or holding civil office under the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: R.36, Mar.1875; R.8, June 1864; others. (P.38, Jan.1890; P.40, Mar.1890.)
